summary: Redwood AE/SE demoed org/project key topology and a capacity simulation in the Console, walked through Optimize batching suggestions, and discussed fallback routing to lower-cost model variants under contention. Customer asked about VPC/on-prem integrations, KMS, SSO, and how to capture billing attribution. Agreed to pilot with capacity spreadsheet and a short benchmark run.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Riley (Redwood SE), Dana (CTO, Mirage), Lee (SRE), Aisha (Product)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to run through a quick simulation of org and project key patterns and how capacity / fallback works in the console. can everyone hear me okay?
[00:08] Dana: yes loud and clear. thanks for squeezing us in, we have about 45 minutes.
[00:12] Riley: great, i'll start with the Console demo then jump into Optimize recommendations — quick note i might flip between tabs.
[00:18] Lee: sounds good, we sent over our p95 traces earlier this morning, hope that came through.
[00:23] Samir: yep we have the CSV, that helped model the traffic for the simulation.
[00:27] [00:30] Riley: (screen) okay i'm on the org topology page, you can see Mirage as the root org, under it we have Projects: web-api, mobile-sdk, analytics-pipeline. i'll show two patterns: one uses org keys that are shared across teams and uses fairshare slices, the other uses project keys keyed to each service.
[00:45] Dana: quick question — in the shared org-key scenario do we get per-team billing breakdown? that's important for chargeback.
[00:50] Riley: good question, yes Console surfaces token-level cost attribution per project id if you include project metadata in the request header. we also demonstrate per-key usage in the billing panel, so you can map keys to internal cost centers. (slight pause) sometimes the label parsing on auto-ingest trips on weird project names — so we usually recommend canonical project keys.
[01:10] Aisha: how hard is it to rotate keys? we want short-lived tokens for dev keys.
[01:14] Samir: rotation is automatic via the keys API, you can set TTLs, and Console will show active/expired tokens. we'll share the key lifecycle doc.
[01:21] [02:00] Riley: moving to capacity simulation — i'm loading the traffic profile for a 30 day window with p95 spikes. watch the right side, there's a capacity slider that allocates X GPUs per org slice and a burst buffer.
[02:12] Lee: is that buffer shared across the org or per-project?
[02:15] Riley: by default the burst buffer is shared at the org level, but you can pin burst lanes to project keys for critical workloads. the simulation shows fairshare enforcement: if web-api exceeds its slice it will get throttled to its fairshare rate while other projects continue.
[02:30] Dana: and if we need guaranteed throughput for payments service we could reserve a dedicated slice?
[02:34] Samir: exactly, we can reserve guaranteed capacity in Dedicated mode for critical projects, and leave less critical traffic on hosted with fallback policies.
[02:40] [03:10] Riley: now i want to trigger a simulated outage — i'm going to reduce available GPUs to 40% and enable autoprov fallback. you should see web-api start to re-route to a lower-cost variant (quantized model) after the fallback threshold.
[03:23] Aisha: lower-cost variant — is the output quality noticeably different? we surface to product.
[03:28] Riley: usually small diffs for short prompt responses; Optimize will show the delta on a small eval set. we'll attach the eval report, but the fallback is configurable — you can choose a model that maintains acceptable latency/quality.
[03:38] Lee: can we enforce sticky routing so payment requests never go to fallback?
[03:42] Riley: yes — sticky routing keys can pin a project key to a model variant and bypass fallback. that is what you'd use for payments.
[03:47] [05:00] Samir: we also wanted to highlight prefix caching and KV cache behavior in the runtime — for completion-heavy workloads caching reduces tokens emitted and improves cost. Riley, want to demo a cache hit example?
[05:12] Riley: sure — demoing Optimize's suggestion engine: it detects repeated prefixes and suggests prefix caching rules. watch the estimated token savings panel — in the simulation it predicts ~22% token savings for analytics-pipeline if we cache intermediate responses.
[05:29] Dana: interesting, that could offset dedicated capacity costs. do you have a breakdown of savings vs batch size?
[05:35] Riley: yes, Optimize recommends batch sizes based on p95 latency SLOs; for our workloads it suggests continuous batching of 8 with a max latency cap of 120ms. i'll export those numbers.
[05:45] [07:15] Aisha: about SSO and account mapping — our security team wants SAML + fine grained RBAC so devs can't access production org keys. how does Redwood handle that?
[07:22] Samir: Console integrates with SAML/SSO; you can map groups to roles and limit access to keys and rollout/console actions. We'll share our SSO mapping example and role matrix.
[07:30] Lee: and for network isolation, we need VPC peering or on-prem option. is Private available in our region?
[07:36] Riley: Private (VPC) is available in east-1 and eu-west-1; we can run an air-gapped on-prem package for regulated workloads. note that VPC still needs our control-plane connection unless fully air-gapped.
[07:47] [09:00] Dana: KMS integration — can we bring our HSM keys for model encryption at rest and for token signing?
[09:06] Riley: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM; for Hosted we offer KMS integrations and envelope encryption. we can provide the KMS integration guide. sometimes names in the guide are wrong, sorry — older doc references HSM vendor that we decommissioned, but we'll send the updated one.
[09:24] [10:40] Riley: (switching tab) back to the simulation, notice the policy panel — there's a canary rollout rule that says: if p95 latency > 400ms for 3 consecutive windows, automatically reduce batch size and enable fallback. you can edit the thresholds.
[10:55] Lee: are the thresholds evaluated per-project or global?
[10:58] Riley: per-routing-group; you can also create org-wide fallbacks. the routing policy engine has precedence: sticky rules > project policies > org fallback.
[11:08] [12:30] Aisha: how does billing work when a request gets routed to a cheaper model? do we get line-items in invoices?
[12:36] Samir: yes invoices show per-model token counts and per-project usage if metadata is provided. the Console billing explorer can slice by model, project, and date.
[12:44] Dana: backup question — we need audit logs for prompt inputs and model responses for compliance. do you retain prompts?
[12:51] Riley: we support configurable retention; for Hosted we can enable prompt logging with redaction. Private gives you full control over retention policies. there's an audit log export. note: some of the auto-transcription in our internal docs says permanent retention by default — that's outdated.
[13:08] [15:00] Samir: i want to role-play a traffic spike — Lee, you'll pretend web-api gets a 3x burst; i'll show how the Console's simulator will allocate fairshare and where throttles occur.
[15:12] Lee: ready.
[15:15] Riley: (simulating) spike incoming — web-api now hits its slice, fairshare soft-limits engage, non-critical requests see 429s, but payment project remains pinned to reserved lane.
[15:30] Aisha: seeing the 429s in the simulator — in reality can we return a custom message to clients instead of generic 429?
[15:35] Riley: yes you can configure custom error bodies and retry-after headers at the API gateway layer. we also have SDK helpers for client-side backoff.
[15:44] Dana: what about concurrency quotas — if mobile spikes in concurrent sessions, will that eat into tokens?
[15:49] Riley: concurrency quotas are separate from token quotas; we enforce them in the routing layer. you can define both per-key.
[16:00] [17:30] Lee: curious about sticky routing under autoscale — if a pinned instance moves to different host, does the sticky route follow?
[17:36] Riley: routing is at the request level — sticky routing uses a mapping stored in the control plane; if instances shift the map still routes to the model variant without dependency on a physical host. there is short-lived state for caching KVs on the host but KV cache warming is automatic on failover.
[17:53] Samir: small caveat — heavy KV cache dependent workloads can see cold-starts on failover, Optimize flags those workloads.
[18:03] Aisha: can Optimize automatically suggest warming policies?
[18:08] Riley: yes, it will suggest pre-warming and recommend a warm-up lambda if your tail is sensitive.
[18:15] [20:00] Dana: for the pilot, we want to test three things: (1) capacity simulation accuracy with our traces, (2) fallback quality delta on our eval prompts, (3) billing attribution per team. is that doable in a 2-week pilot?
[20:12] Samir: yes, that's exactly what most pilots aim for. we'll scope a skinny pilot: ingest your traces, run a benchmark against 2 model variants, and produce a short cost/quality report.
[20:22] Lee: what access do you need for ingesting traces? can we share S3 link?
[20:26] Riley: S3 link works — we'll pull the CSVs. for sensitive data we can have you upload to a temporary private bucket in our VPC, or you can obfuscate traces.
[20:33] Dana: we prefer to obfuscate first.
[20:36] Samir: cool, we'll provide the format spec.
[20:40] [22:00] Riley: quick note on model scheduling — if a model variant is CPU-quantized it might not be compatible with very short prompt latencies; the scheduler uses model capability tags to determine routing eligibility. sometimes our auto-tagging mislabels older forks, so we recommend pinning models in production configs.
[22:22] Aisha: does Redwood Optimize recommend quantization profiles?
[22:25] Riley: yes, Optimize will suggest quantization levels and show expected latency/cost tradeoffs. it outputs a recommendation you can accept or tweak.
[22:32] [24:00] Samir: security question — we mentioned SAML, KMS, audit logs — anything else from your security team?
[24:07] Dana: data residency concerns — EU data must remain in eu-west. will the fallback ever cross region?
[24:14] Riley: routing policies honor data-residency constraints; fallback respects region boundaries unless you explicitly enable cross-region failover. we tend to leave that off for regulated workloads.
[24:22] Lee: do you provide signed runbooks for audit?
[24:26] Samir: yes enterprise customers get a runbook and compliance bundle.
[24:30] [26:00] Riley: showing Console's policy editor now — you can author routing rules in a form or YAML. i'll create a rule: if org p95 > 350ms then switch analytics to variant q-2 and reduce batch to 4. saving now.
[26:15] Aisha: will that combo create a visible diff in the eval dashboard?
[26:18] Riley: yes, the eval job runs against the active rollout and shows latency and quality score deltas. you can schedule evals pre/post rollout.
[26:28] [28:00] Dana: question on SLAs — what uptime guarantees for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[28:07] Samir: Hosted has a best-effort SLA with status dashboard; Dedicated includes an SLA with monthly uptime and latency targets. we'll attach the SLA doc.
[28:16] Lee: and what about incident response and escalation?
[28:19] Riley: enterprise plans include a dedicated TAM and a priority Support channel; P1 escalations have a response SLA.
[28:28] [30:00] Aisha: okay this is great. next steps, can we get a small benchmark run with our 50k sample prompts?
[30:07] Samir: absolutely — we'll run a benchmark with two model variants and share the eval. Riley, can you confirm the time to run that?
[30:14] Riley: if the data is ready, 24-48 hours for an initial run. for full 50k it might be 72 hours depending on queue.
[30:22] Dana: and cost for that run?
[30:25] Samir: we can cover a small pilot; for larger runs we'll propose a pilot credit or dedicated bench slot.
[30:31] [32:00] Riley: last demo bit — Console audit trail shows who changed a routing policy and when. it attaches diffs and the user id; this helps during incident postmortems.
[32:12] Lee: good. we'll need retention of at least 90 days for diffs.
[32:17] Samir: noted, retention policy is configurable.
[32:22] [34:00] Dana: any gotchas we should know before we start pilot?
[34:06] Riley: a few: (1) make sure project metadata is consistent across services so attribution works; (2) avoid mixing legacy keys with auto-renewed keys during pilot; (3) if you use heavy KV cache patterns test for warm-start behavior.
[34:22] Aisha: that's helpful — we'll align with our infra runbook.
[34:26] [36:00] Samir: ok recap — we demoed org/project topologies, capacity simulation, fallback routing, Optimize suggestions, and security options. next steps: Samir sends capacity spreadsheet and pricing, Riley sends Console screenshots + SSO/KMS docs, Lee/Aisha to provide obfuscated traces and availability for pilot.
[36:20] Dana: thanks, that's our side. can you also include a short checklist for pilot acceptance criteria?
[36:27] Samir: yes we'll propose acceptance criteria: simulator accuracy within 10% of observed p95, fallback quality delta under 5% for critical prompts, billing attribution validated for three projects.
[36:40] [38:00] Riley: i'll also attach a small runbook for key rotation and a sample YAML routing rule.
[38:10] Lee: will you share the Console link for the simulation so we can poke around?
[38:14] Riley: yes, sharing link now — [link: https://app.redwood.ai/console/sim/ff-20260505] (link shared in chat).
[38:22] Dana: great. last quick ask: do you support token masking in logs? we want to mask PII.
[38:28] Riley: yes, we support token-level redaction and field-based redaction before storage. we'll document patterns.
[38:36] [40:00] Samir: any final questions?
[40:05] Aisha: none from me. excited to run the pilot.
[40:08] Lee: none.
[40:10] Dana: good session, thanks both.
[40:15] Samir: thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts and formal pilot scope.
[40:20] [END]
